item.title: Bank Marketing - Part 1 - Making the call - An Exploratory Data Analysis
item.description:
Other posts in this series:

  • Bank Marketing - Part 2 - Who will say yes? - Building Classification Models
  • Bank Marketing - Part 3 - Keeping up with the times - Sliding Window Models

A Portuguese bank ran a series of telemarketing campaigns between May 2008 and November 2010. Its staff called clients and asked them to open a term deposit, a savings account that pays a fixed interest rate for a fixed period. The Bank Marketing dataset (Moro, Cortez and Rita, 2014) records 41,188 of these calls: who the client was, how and when they were called, the state of the economy at the time, and whether the client said yes.

In the Ames Housing and Diamonds case studies, we predicted a number (a price). Here, we predict a category: will a client subscribe, yes or no? This kind of problem is called classification. The case study has three posts:

  1. In this post, we explore the data to find which features affect whether a client subscribes, and we prepare the data for models. An exploratory data analysis (EDA) is the first study of a dataset before we build models.
  2. In Part 2, we build models that predict which clients will subscribe, and we find out how a bank could use them to decide whom to call.
  3. In Part 3, we train the models on a sliding window of recent months and predict the next month, as a bank would do in practice.

Data Description

Each row is one call, which was the last call to a client in a campaign. The rows are in the order of the calls, from May 2008 to November 2010. There are 20 features and the target, y, which is the value that we want to predict:

dfDescription <- tribble(~ Feature, ~ Type, ~ Description,
                         "age", "numerical", "age of the client",
                         "job", "categorical", "type of job",
                         "marital", "categorical", "marital status (*divorced* also means widowed)",
                         "education", "categorical", "highest level of education",
                         "default", "categorical", "does the client have a loan in default?",
                         "housing", "categorical", "does the client have a housing loan?",
                         "loan", "categorical", "does the client have a personal loan?",
                         "contact", "categorical", "type of phone: cellular or telephone (landline)",
                         "month", "categorical", "month of the call",
                         "day_of_week", "categorical", "day of the week of the call",
                         "duration", "numerical", "length of the call, in seconds",
                         "campaign", "numerical", "number of calls to the client in this campaign, including this one",
                         "pdays", "numerical", "days since the client was last called in a previous campaign (999: not called)",
                         "previous", "numerical", "number of calls to the client before this campaign",
                         "poutcome", "categorical", "result of the previous campaign",
                         "emp.var.rate", "numerical", "employment variation rate (quarterly)",
                         "cons.price.idx", "numerical", "consumer price index (monthly)",
                         "cons.conf.idx", "numerical", "consumer confidence index (monthly)",
                         "euribor3m", "numerical", "3 month Euribor interest rate (daily)",
                         "nr.employed", "numerical", "number of employees in the economy, in thousands (quarterly)",
                         "y", "categorical", "**target**: did the client subscribe to a term deposit?")

knitr::kable(dfDescription)
Feature Type Description
age numerical age of the client
job categorical type of job
marital categorical marital status (divorced also means widowed)
education categorical highest level of education
default categorical does the client have a loan in default?
housing categorical does the client have a housing loan?
loan categorical does the client have a personal loan?
contact categorical type of phone: cellular or telephone (landline)
month categorical month of the call
day_of_week categorical day of the week of the call
duration numerical length of the call, in seconds
campaign numerical number of calls to the client in this campaign, including this one
pdays numerical days since the client was last called in a previous campaign (999: not called)
previous numerical number of calls to the client before this campaign
poutcome categorical result of the previous campaign
emp.var.rate numerical employment variation rate (quarterly)
cons.price.idx numerical consumer price index (monthly)
cons.conf.idx numerical consumer confidence index (monthly)
euribor3m numerical 3 month Euribor interest rate (daily)
nr.employed numerical number of employees in the economy, in thousands (quarterly)
y categorical target: did the client subscribe to a term deposit?

The last five features describe the economy of Portugal at the time of the call. They are the same for all the clients who were called on the same day.

Data Quality

Before we explore the features, we check the data for problems.

# exact duplicate rows
nDuplicates <- sum(duplicated(dfRaw))

# number of "unknown" values in each categorical feature
dfUnknown <- dfRaw %>%
  select(where(is.character)) %>%
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(.x == "unknown"))) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "feature", values_to = "unknown") %>%
  filter(unknown > 0) %>%
  mutate(percent = round(100 * unknown / nrow(dfRaw), 1)) %>%
  arrange(desc(unknown))

knitr::kable(dfUnknown, col.names = c("Feature", "Unknown values", "% of calls"))
Feature Unknown values % of calls
default 8597 20.9
education 1731 4.2
housing 990 2.4
loan 990 2.4
job 330 0.8
marital 80 0.2 
# clients called in a previous campaign, by whether pdays is recorded
dfPrevious <- dfRaw %>%
  filter(previous > 0) %>%
  count(pdays_recorded = pdays != 999, poutcome)

What’s notable?

  • There are no empty (missing) values. Instead, the categorical features use the category unknown. default is unknown for 20.9% of the clients. housing and loan are unknown for the same 990 clients.
  • 12 rows are exact copies of other rows. The data has no client ID, so we cannot tell whether these are the same call recorded twice or different clients with the same details. They are too few to matter, and we remove them when we prepare the data.
  • default has only 3 clients with yes. So the feature really tells us whether the client’s answer was no or unknown.
  • The description says that a pdays of 999 means the client was not called before. But 5,625 clients were called in a previous campaign (previous is more than 0), and only 1,515 of them have a pdays value. Of those, 1373 had a successful previous campaign. So pdays is mostly recorded for clients who said yes before.

The Target: Who Subscribed?

dfTarget <- dfRaw %>% count(y) %>% mutate(percent = 100 * n / sum(n))
rate_yes <- mean(dfRaw$y == "yes")

ggplot(dfTarget, aes(x = y, y = n, fill = y)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = glue::glue("{format(n, big.mark = ',')} ({round(percent, 1)}%)")), vjust = -0.5, family = "Roboto Condensed") +
  scale_fill_quant(palette = "main") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.1))) +
  labs(x = "Subscribed to a term deposit (y)", y = "Number of calls", title = "Most clients said no")

What’s notable?

  • Only 11.3% of the calls ended with a subscription. The two classes are very unequal in size (imbalanced).
  • So a model that always predicts no would be right 88.7% of the time, but it would be useless. In Part 2, we use measures that are not fooled by this.

In the rest of this post, we compare the subscription rate, the percentage of calls that ended with a yes, across the values of each feature. The dashed line in the plots is the overall rate of 11.3%. These functions make the plots:

# subscription rate and number of calls for each category of a feature
plot_rate <- function(df, feature, sortByRate = TRUE, minCount = 30) {
  dfRate <- df %>%
    group_by(category = .data[[feature]]) %>%
    summarise(calls = n(), rate = mean(y == "yes"), .groups = "drop") %>%
    filter(calls >= minCount)
  if (sortByRate) dfRate <- dfRate %>% mutate(category = fct_reorder(as.factor(category), rate))
  ggplot(dfRate, aes(x = category, y = rate)) +
    geom_col(fill = "#00AED8") +
    geom_hline(yintercept = mean(df$y == "yes"), lty = 2) +
    geom_text(aes(label = scales::label_comma()(calls)), hjust = -0.1, size = 3, family = "Roboto Condensed") +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent(), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.25))) +
    coord_flip() +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "Subscription rate", title = feature)
}

# subscription rate for bins of a numerical feature
plot_rate_bins <- function(df, feature, breaks, labels = NULL) {
  df %>%
    mutate(bin = cut(.data[[feature]], breaks = breaks, labels = labels, include.lowest = TRUE, dig.lab = 5)) %>%
    plot_rate("bin", sortByRate = FALSE) +
    labs(title = feature)
}

The numbers next to the bars are the numbers of calls. Categories with fewer than 30 calls are not shown, because their rates are not reliable.

A Feature We Cannot Use: Call Duration

plot_rate_bins(dfRaw, "duration", breaks = c(0, 60, 120, 180, 300, 600, 5000)) +
  labs(x = "Length of the call (seconds)")

What’s notable?

  • duration predicts the result very well: almost no client who talked for less than a minute subscribed, and about half of the clients who talked for more than 10 minutes did.
  • But we only know the length of a call after the call has ended, and by then we also know whether the client said yes. A bank cannot use it to decide whom to call. Using a feature that would not be known at the time of the prediction is called data leakage. It makes a model look much better than it will be in practice.
  • The authors of the dataset give the same warning. So we drop duration.

Univariate Analysis: One Feature at a Time

Numerical Features

vFeaturesNumRaw <- c("age", "campaign", "previous", "emp.var.rate", "cons.price.idx", "cons.conf.idx", "euribor3m", "nr.employed")
eda_plot_histograms(dfRaw, vFeaturesNumRaw, nCols = 4)

What’s notable?

  • Most clients are between 30 and 50 years old.
  • Most clients were called once or twice in the campaign, but some were called up to 56 times. campaign is very skewed.
  • Most clients (86%) were never called in a previous campaign.
  • The economic features have only a few distinct values, with gaps between them. For example, nr.employed has only 11 values, because it changes once a quarter. So these features also tell us when a call was made.

Categorical Features

vFeaturesCatRaw <- c("job", "marital", "education", "default", "housing", "loan", "contact", "month", "day_of_week", "poutcome")
cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = map(vFeaturesCatRaw, ~ eda_plot_column(dfRaw, .x)), ncol = 3)

What’s notable?

  • Most clients work in administration, blue-collar jobs or as technicians.
  • Most calls were made in May, and the fewest in December and March. There are no calls in January and February.
  • About two thirds of the calls were to cell phones.

Bivariate Analysis: Each Feature and the Subscription Rate

Client Features

p1 <- plot_rate_bins(dfRaw, "age", breaks = c(17, 25, 30, 40, 50, 60, 100))
p2 <- plot_rate(dfRaw, "job")
p3 <- plot_rate(dfRaw, "marital")
p4 <- plot_rate(dfRaw, "education")
p5 <- plot_rate(dfRaw, "default")
p6 <- plot_rate(dfRaw, "housing")
cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = list(p1, p2, p3, p4, p5, p6), ncol = 2)

What’s notable?

  • The youngest and the oldest clients are the most likely to subscribe: students and retired people subscribe at more than twice the overall rate. Blue-collar workers subscribe the least.
  • Clients with a university degree subscribe more often than clients with a basic education.
  • Clients whose default status is unknown subscribe much less often than clients who said they have no loan in default.
  • Having a housing loan (and, not shown, a personal loan) makes almost no difference.

Campaign Features

dfMonthOrder <- dfRaw %>% mutate(month = factor(month, levels = c("mar","apr","may","jun","jul","aug","sep","oct","nov","dec")),
                                 day_of_week = factor(day_of_week, levels = c("mon","tue","wed","thu","fri")))
p1 <- plot_rate(dfRaw, "contact")
p2 <- plot_rate(dfMonthOrder, "month", sortByRate = FALSE)
p3 <- plot_rate(dfMonthOrder, "day_of_week", sortByRate = FALSE)
p4 <- plot_rate_bins(dfRaw, "campaign", breaks = c(1, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5, 5.5, 10.5, 60), labels = c("1", "2", "3", "4-5", "6-10", "11+")) +
  labs(title = "campaign (calls in this campaign)")
p5 <- plot_rate_bins(dfRaw, "previous", breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 10), labels = c("0", "1", "2", "3+")) +
  labs(title = "previous (calls before this campaign)")
p6 <- plot_rate(dfRaw, "poutcome")
cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = list(p1, p2, p3, p4, p5, p6), ncol = 2)

What’s notable?

  • Clients called on a cell phone subscribe almost three times as often as clients called on a landline.
  • The months with the fewest calls (March, September, October and December) have the highest rates, close to 50%. May, the busiest month, has the lowest rate. We look at this again in the next section.
  • The day of the week makes little difference.
  • Each extra call in the same campaign makes a yes less likely. Only 3% of the clients who were called more than 10 times subscribed.
  • The more often a client was called in previous campaigns, the more likely a yes: these clients already know the bank.
  • The result of the previous campaign is the strongest client-level signal: 65% of the clients who said yes before said yes again.

The Economy and the Time of the Call

The rows are in the order of the calls. So we can follow the subscription rate over time. Here, we split the calls into blocks of 1,000 consecutive calls:

dfTime <- dfRaw %>%
  mutate(call_order = row_number(), block = (call_order - 1) %/% 1000 + 1) %>%
  group_by(block) %>%
  summarise(first_call = min(call_order), rate = mean(y == "yes"), euribor3m = mean(euribor3m), nr.employed = mean(nr.employed))

p1 <- ggplot(dfTime, aes(x = first_call, y = rate)) +
  geom_line(color = "#00AED8") + geom_point(color = "#00AED8") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Subscription rate", title = "Subscription rate in each block of 1,000 calls")
p2 <- ggplot(dfTime, aes(x = first_call, y = euribor3m)) +
  geom_line(color = "#F37735") + geom_point(color = "#F37735") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  labs(x = "Call number (in order of time)", y = "3 month Euribor (%)", title = "Interest rate at the time of the calls")
cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = list(p1, p2), ncol = 1, align = "v")

eda_plot_correlation_matrix(dfRaw %>% select(emp.var.rate, cons.price.idx, cons.conf.idx, euribor3m, nr.employed),
                            plotTitle = "Correlation of the economic features")

What’s notable?

  • In the first 23,000 or so calls, fewer than 1 in 10 calls ended with a yes. After the interest rate fell in late 2008 and 2009, the rate rose, and in the last blocks about half of the calls were successful. Fewer calls were made in that period, which explains why the quiet months had the highest rates.
  • euribor3m, emp.var.rate and nr.employed move together (their correlations are above 0.9). They describe the same economic cycle.
  • So the economic features are strong predictors, but much of their power comes from telling the model when the call was made. A model can learn that calls in a certain period were successful. That is useful when we predict calls from the same period, but the economy of the next campaign will be different. In Part 2, we test the models on calls from the same period, and then on later calls.

When Was Each Call Made?

The data gives the month and the day of the week of each call, but not the year. We can recover the year from the order of the calls. There are no calls in January or February, so a new year starts wherever the month goes back to an earlier month (for example, from December to March). The first call was made in May 2008.

dfDates <- dfRaw %>%
  mutate(Id = row_number(),
         month_num = match(month, tolower(month.abb)),
         year = 2008 + cumsum(c(0, diff(month_num) < 0)),
         year_month = as.Date(sprintf("%d-%02d-01", year, month_num)))

# the rows where a new year starts
dfDates %>%
  filter(c(FALSE, diff(month_num) < 0)) %>%
  transmute(`Call number` = Id, `Month` = month, `Year` = year) %>%
  knitr::kable()
Call number Month Year
27691 mar 2009
39131 mar 2010 
# the consumer price and confidence indices change once a month: check that each reconstructed month has a single
# value of each, and that each month has a different value
dfMonthCheck <- dfDates %>%
  group_by(year_month) %>%
  summarise(calls = n(), rate = mean(y == "yes"),
            price_values = n_distinct(cons.price.idx), confidence_values = n_distinct(cons.conf.idx),
            cons.price.idx = first(cons.price.idx))

There are 3 years and 26 months, from May 2008 to November 2010, as in the description of the dataset. We can check the result with the monthly economic features. In each of the 26 months, cons.price.idx and cons.conf.idx have exactly one value, and the 26 months have 26 different consumer price indices. So the years are right.

p1 <- ggplot(dfMonthCheck, aes(x = year_month, y = calls)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#00AED8") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma()) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "3 months", date_labels = "%b %Y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Calls", title = "Number of calls in each month")
p2 <- ggplot(dfMonthCheck, aes(x = year_month, y = rate)) +
  geom_line(color = "#F37735") + geom_point(aes(size = calls), color = "#F37735", show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_percent()) +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "3 months", date_labels = "%b %Y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Subscription rate", title = "Subscription rate in each month (point size: number of calls)")
cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = list(p1, p2), ncol = 1, align = "v")

# share of the calls made in 2008, and the calls in October and December 2008
pct_2008 <- round(100 * mean(dfDates$year == 2008))
calls_oct_dec_2008 <- sum(dfMonthCheck$calls[dfMonthCheck$year_month %in% as.Date(c("2008-10-01", "2008-12-01"))])

What’s notable?

  • 67% of the calls were made in 2008, when fewer than 1 in 15 calls succeeded, except in October and December, which had only 77 calls between them.
  • From the middle of 2009, the bank made far fewer calls, and more of them succeeded: in 2010, about half of the calls ended with a yes. Part of this change may come from the economy, and part from the bank calling different clients. The data cannot separate the two.
  • So the behavior of clients changed over time. A model that learns from the past should give more weight to the recent past. In Part 3, we train the models on a sliding window of recent months, and predict the next month.

Associations Between Features

Correlation only works for numerical features. To compare all the features at once, including the categorical ones and the target, we use an association matrix. It uses Cramér’s V for pairs of categorical features: 0 means no association and 1 means that one feature completely determines the other.

dfAssoc <- dfRaw %>%
  select(-duration) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.character), as.factor))
eda_plot_association_matrix(dfAssoc, outlineVar = "y", plotTitle = "Association of features with each other and with y")

What’s notable?

  • The target y is most strongly associated with the economic features (about 0.3), with poutcome, pdays and previous (the history of previous campaigns), and with month. job and contact follow, with about 0.15.
  • pdays, previous and poutcome are strongly associated with each other, because they all describe the previous campaign.
  • month, contact and the economic features are strongly associated with each other, because they all depend on when the call was made.
  • age is associated with job and marital: students are young, and retired people are old.
  • housing and loan are almost unrelated to y. They are associated with each other only because their unknown values are the same clients.

Preparing the Data for Models

Based on what we have found, we make these changes:

  • Remove the 12 duplicate rows.
  • Drop duration, which is not known before a call (data leakage).
  • Replace pdays with a yes/no feature, recent_contact, that says whether pdays was recorded. Its exact value adds little, because it is recorded almost only for clients with a successful previous campaign, and the value 999 would mislead a linear model.
  • Change the 3 yes answers in default to unknown, so that the feature compares clients who said no with all the others. Three examples are too few for a model to learn from.
  • Keep unknown as a category in the other features, because it is informative: for example, clients whose education is unknown subscribe more often than average.
  • Put the months and the days of the week in calendar order.
  • Add an Id that keeps the order of the calls, so that in Part 2 we can test the models on later calls. The models do not use it as a feature.
  • Keep the year and the month of each call in a separate table, dfCallDates, for the sliding windows of Part 3. They are not features either, because they would tell a model directly when a call was made.

Then we set aside 25% of the calls as a testing set, which the models will not see while they learn. We use stratified sampling, so that the testing set has the same subscription rate as the training set.

dfClean <- dfRaw %>%
  mutate(Id = row_number()) %>%
  filter(!duplicated(pick(-Id))) %>%
  select(-duration) %>%
  mutate(recent_contact = if_else(pdays != 999, "yes", "no"),
         default = if_else(default == "yes", "unknown", default),
         month = factor(month, levels = c("mar","apr","may","jun","jul","aug","sep","oct","nov","dec")),
         day_of_week = factor(day_of_week, levels = c("mon","tue","wed","thu","fri")),
         y = factor(y, levels = c("yes", "no"))) %>%
  select(-pdays) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.character), as.factor)) %>%
  select(Id, y, everything())

vFeaturesNum <- dfClean %>% select(-Id, -y) %>% select(where(is.numeric)) %>% colnames()
vFeaturesCat <- dfClean %>% select(-Id, -y) %>% select(where(is.factor)) %>% colnames()

# stratified split into training (75%) and testing (25%) sets
set.seed(2300)
data_split <- initial_split(dfClean, prop = 0.75, strata = y)
vTestIDs <- testing(data_split)$Id

dfSplit <- dfClean %>%
  mutate(set = if_else(Id %in% vTestIDs, "testing", "training")) %>%
  group_by(set) %>%
  summarise(calls = n(), subscribed = sum(y == "yes"), rate = round(100 * mean(y == "yes"), 2))
knitr::kable(dfSplit, col.names = c("Set", "Calls", "Subscribed", "Subscription rate (%)"))
Set Calls Subscribed Subscription rate (%)
testing 10295 1160 11.27
training 30881 3479 11.27 
# the year and month of each call that is kept, for the sliding windows of Part 3
dfCallDates <- dfDates %>%
  filter(Id %in% dfClean$Id) %>%
  select(Id, year, year_month)

save(dfClean, vTestIDs, vFeaturesNum, vFeaturesCat, dfCallDates, file = "Bank_Marketing_Clean.Rda")

The finalized dataset has 41,176 calls and 19 features: 8 numerical and 11 categorical.

Next Steps

We have learned that:

  • The history of a client with the bank (poutcome, previous) and the type of phone are strong signals.
  • The economy and the time of the call matter a lot, so we must be careful about how we test the models.
  • Age and job matter, but less.
  • duration must not be used, even though it looks like the best predictor.

In Part 2, we use this dataset to build models that predict which clients will subscribe. In Part 3, we use the dates of the calls to train the models on recent months only.

item.title: Ames Housing - Part 2 - Walkthrough - An Exploratory Data Analysis
item.description:
Other posts in this series:

  • Ames Housing - Part 1 - Laying the foundation - Building a Data Pipeline
  • Ames Housing - Part 3 - Closing the deal - Building Models

In Part 1, we built a data pipeline that cleans the Ames Housing dataset and creates new features. In this post, we explore the finalized dataset. An exploratory data analysis (EDA) is the first study of a dataset before we build models. We look at the features one at a time, then two and three at a time, to find which features affect the sale price. In Part 3, we use what we learn to build models.

Univariate Analysis: One Feature at a Time

In this section, we look at each feature by itself.

Numerical Features

First, let’s plot all the features that measure an area in square feet:

eda_plot_histograms(dfClean, vFeaturesNum[str_detect(vFeaturesNum, "SF|Area")])

What’s notable?

  • All the area features have outliers, which are values that are very different from most other values.
  • Many features are very skewed: most values are small and a few values are much larger. Before we build models, we must transform these features (for example, with a log) to make them less skewed.

Now let’s look at the other numerical features:

eda_plot_histograms(dfClean, setdiff(vFeaturesNum[!str_detect(vFeaturesNum, "SF|Area")], "SalePrice"))

What’s notable?

  • Most properties were sold less than 20 years after they were built or remodeled.

Let’s plot SalePrice on a log scale. On a log scale, each step on the axis multiplies the value by the same amount:

eda_plot_histograms(dfClean, "SalePrice", nBins = 50, xLog = T, xLabelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1))

What’s notable?

  • The distribution has long tails on both sides: a few properties are much cheaper or much more expensive than most.
  • 11 properties cost less than USD 50,000, and 17 properties cost more than USD 500,000.
  • Outliers have a strong effect on linear models.

Categorical Features

Ordinal Features

cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = map(vFeaturesCat1, ~ eda_plot_column(dfClean, .x)), ncol = 4)

What’s notable?

  • In many features, 1 or 2 categories are much more common than the others. This makes these features hard to use for predictions, because the data has only a few examples of the other categories.

Nominal Features.

cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = map(vFeaturesCat2, ~ eda_plot_column(dfClean, .x)), ncol = 4)

What’s notable?

  • In many features, 1 or 2 categories are much more common than the others.
  • Most properties are sold in the summer months, and the fewest in the winter months.
  • The data shows the effect of the housing market crisis: the fewest properties were sold in 2010.

Bivariate Analysis: Two Features at a Time

Numerical-Numerical

Let’s look at how SalePrice changes with each of the other numerical features. A scatter plot shows one dot for each property, and the line shows the best straight line through the dots (a regression line):

eda_plot_scatter(dfClean, vFeaturesNum, "SalePrice", yLabelsScale = scales::dollar)

Let’s look more closely at TotalSF. The labels show the properties with the largest Cook’s distance. Cook’s distance measures how much one point pulls the regression line towards itself:

eda_plot_scatter(dfClean, "TotalSF", "SalePrice", yLabelsScale = scales::dollar,
                 nLabel = 3, feature_id = "Id", labelBy = "cooks")

# Cook's distance of each property in a linear fit of SalePrice on TotalSF
dfInfluence <- dfClean %>% select(Id, TotalSF, SalePrice) %>% drop_na()
dfInfluence <- dfInfluence %>%
  mutate(cooks = cooks.distance(lm(SalePrice ~ TotalSF, data = dfInfluence))) %>%
  arrange(desc(cooks))

vOutliers_TotalSF <- dfInfluence$Id[1:3]

What’s notable?

  • The scatter plot of TotalSF and SalePrice clearly shows a few very large properties that sold at unusually low prices. These points have high leverage: they are far from the other points, so they pull the regression line strongly. Without them, the line would be steeper.
  • The same properties also affect TotalBsmtSF.
  • The Ids of these properties are 1299,2550,524. Their Cook’s distances are 5.69, 2.46, 0.54. These values are much higher than the usual limit of 4/n = 0.0014, where n is the number of properties. The next property has a Cook’s distance of only 0.12. Of these three properties, 524 and 1299 are in the training set.

Transforming Skewed Features

Many numerical features are right skewed. Can we change them with a simple formula (a transform), so that their relationship with log(SalePrice) becomes closer to a straight line? Let’s compare common transforms of three features: TotalSF, the strongest area feature; LotArea, which is very skewed; and GarageArea, which is almost not skewed. Each panel shows the R-squared of a straight line through the points. R-squared is a number from 0 to 1. It tells how much of the variation in log(SalePrice) the line explains:

lTransformPlots <- map(c("TotalSF", "LotArea", "GarageArea"), ~ eda_plot_transforms(dfClean, .x, "SalePrice"))
cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = lTransformPlots, ncol = 1)

# R-squared of each transform, in the order of the panels
vR2 <- map(lTransformPlots, ~ .x$data %>%
             distinct(transform, r_squared) %>%
             pull(r_squared) %>%
             set_names(c("identity", "log", "sqrt", "cuberoot"))) %>%
  set_names(c("TotalSF", "LotArea", "GarageArea"))
r2 <- function(feature, transform) round(vR2[[feature]][transform], 3)

# skewness of each feature
vSkew <- map_dbl(c(TotalSF = "TotalSF", LotArea = "LotArea", GarageArea = "GarageArea"), ~ timeDate::skewness(dfClean[[.x]], na.rm = T))

What’s notable?

  • A log transform almost doubles the R-squared of LotArea (skewness 12.8), from 0.066 to 0.138. Without the transform, a few very large lots control the line. The log makes these large values smaller.
  • All the transforms improve TotalSF (skewness 1.5) a little. With a log, the R-squared goes from 0.61 to 0.647.
  • GarageArea (skewness 0.2) is almost not skewed, and the transforms make the fit worse. With a log, the R-squared goes down from 0.426 to 0.389. Also, the log cannot use the properties without a garage, because the log of 0 does not exist.
  • So, before we build linear models, we should transform only the very skewed features, not all of them.

Correlations with SalePrice

We keep the features whose correlation with SalePrice is at least 0.1 or at most -0.1. The Pearson correlation measures how close a relationship is to a straight line, so outliers and skewed features affect it strongly. The Spearman correlation uses the ranks of the values (1st, 2nd, 3rd, …) instead of the values. So it measures whether one feature always goes up (or always goes down) when the other goes up, even along a curve. If we compare the two, we can see which relationships are strong but not straight lines:

library(corrr)

dfCor <- dfClean[vFeaturesNum] %>% 
  correlate() %>% 
  focus(SalePrice) %>% 
  dplyr::rename(feature = term,
                corr = SalePrice) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(corr))) %>% 
  dplyr::filter(abs(corr) > 0.1) %>% 
  mutate(corr = round(corr, 2)) %>% 
  mutate(feature = fct_reorder(feature, corr)) %>% 
  dplyr::filter(!(feature %in% vFeatures_to_exclude))

vFeaturesCor <- dfCor %>% pull(feature) %>% as.character()

p1 <- eda_plot_target_correlations(dfClean[vFeaturesNum], "SalePrice", method = "pearson", minAbsCor = 0.1)
p2 <- eda_plot_target_correlations(dfClean[vFeaturesNum], "SalePrice", method = "spearman", minAbsCor = 0.1)
cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = list(p1, p2), ncol = 2)

# compare Pearson and Spearman correlations
dfCorMethods <- tibble(feature = setdiff(vFeaturesNum, "SalePrice")) %>%
  mutate(pearson = map_dbl(feature, ~ cor(dfClean[[.x]], dfClean$SalePrice, use = "pairwise.complete.obs")),
         spearman = map_dbl(feature, ~ cor(dfClean[[.x]], dfClean$SalePrice, use = "pairwise.complete.obs", method = "spearman")))
cor_of <- function(feature_name, method) round(dfCorMethods[[method]][dfCorMethods$feature == feature_name], 2)

What’s notable?

  • The 5 most correlated features are TotalSF, GarageArea, TotalBath, TotalBsmtSF, 1stFlrSF. A buyer would naturally look at these features to judge a property and its price.
  • PropertyAge has a strong negative correlation with SalePrice. This means that newer properties sell for higher prices than older properties.
  • For most features, the Pearson and Spearman correlations are similar. But LotArea is different: its correlation goes up from 0.27 to 0.43. Larger lots do sell for more, but the relationship is far from a straight line. The log transform above partly corrects this.
  • For BsmtFinSF1, the correlation goes down from 0.43 to 0.33. About 32% of the properties have no finished basement, so they all have the same rank. Also, the largest finished basements have a large effect on the Pearson correlation. So the straight-line relationship with SalePrice seems stronger than the rank relationship.

Numerical-Categorical (Ordinal)

cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist=map2(vFeaturesCat1,"SalePrice", ~ eda_plot_box(dfClean, .x, .y, yLimits = c(35000,410000))), ncol = 4)

What’s notable?

  • In almost all of these features, SalePrice clearly changes with the order of the categories.
  • The overall quality and the exterior quality show some of the strongest trends.

Numerical-Categorical (Nominal)

Now let’s look at SalePrice for the nominal features. The categories of a nominal feature have no natural order. But if we sort the categories by their median SalePrice, we can find trends. To show the trends better, the SalePrice axis does not show the outliers. A box plot shows the middle half of the prices as a box, with a line at the median:

cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist=map2(vFeaturesCat2,"SalePrice", ~ eda_plot_box(dfClean, .x, .y, yLimits = c(35000,410000))), ncol = 4)

What’s notable?

  • GarageType: buyers prefer built-in and attached garages to detached garages and other types.
  • The categories of MSSubClass show that houses built in 1946 or later have higher prices than older houses.

Multivariate Analysis: Three or More Features at a Time

In this section, we look at how some related features change SalePrice together.

Numerical-Numerical-Categorical

TotalSF and GarageArea have some of the strongest correlations with SalePrice. Let’s see how these relationships change with NeighborhoodType and GarageType:

p1 <- eda_plot_scatter_cat(dfClean, "TotalSF", "SalePrice", "NeighborhoodType", yLabelsScale = scales::dollar)
p2 <- eda_plot_scatter_cat(dfClean, "GarageArea", "SalePrice", "GarageType", yLabelsScale = scales::dollar)
cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = list(p1, p2), ncol = 1)

  • For the same total area, properties in some neighborhoods sell for more than in others.
  • The properties without a garage form a separate group.
  • For the same GarageArea, properties with built-in or attached garages usually sell for more.
  • So NeighborhoodType and GarageType explain some of the differences in SalePrice.

Categorical-Numerical-Numerical

The dots in the scatter plots overlap a lot. So let’s check these results in another way, and compare categories among properties of similar size. We split TotalSF and GarageArea into four groups (bins) with the same number of properties. Then we plot SalePrice for each category in each group. We also check whether central air conditioning (CentralAir) changes the price of properties of the same size:

p1 <- eda_plot_box_by_bins(dfClean, "NeighborhoodType", "SalePrice", "TotalSF", yLog = T, yLabelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1))
p2 <- eda_plot_box_by_bins(dfClean, "GarageType", "SalePrice", "GarageArea", yLog = T, yLabelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1))
p3 <- eda_plot_box_by_bins(dfClean, "CentralAir", "SalePrice", "TotalSF", yLog = T, yLabelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1))
cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = list(p1, p2, p3), ncol = 1)

# median SalePrice by category within each bin
get_bin_medians <- function(p) {
  p$data %>%
    group_by(bin = as.integer(bin), category = as.character(x)) %>%
    summarise(median = median(y), .groups = "drop")
}
lBinMedians <- map(list(neighborhood = p1, garage = p2, air = p3), get_bin_medians)
bin_median <- function(plotName, binNum, categoryName) {
  dfMedians <- lBinMedians[[plotName]]
  scales::dollar(dfMedians$median[dfMedians$bin == binNum & dfMedians$category == categoryName], accuracy = 1)
}

What’s notable?

  • The neighborhood is very important, even for properties of the same size. For the largest properties, the median SalePrice goes from $161,000 in Type5 neighborhoods to $327,000 in Type1 neighborhoods. Type1 neighborhoods have few or no properties in the smallest group, so the neighborhood and the size are also related.
  • For the same GarageArea, built-in and attached garages go with higher prices than detached garages. For the largest garages, the median SalePrice is $299,018 for built-in garages, $253,000 for attached garages and $140,000 for detached garages. Some garage types have very few properties, so their box plots are less reliable.
  • Properties with central air conditioning sell for more, at every size. For the largest properties, the median SalePrice is $262,140 with central air and $136,000 without it.

Categorical-Categorical-Numerical

Does a combination of two categorical features tell us more about SalePrice? A heatmap answers this question. It is a grid of tiles, one tile for each combination of two categories:

p1 <- eda_plot_heatmap(dfClean, "OverallQual", "NeighborhoodType", "SalePrice")
p2 <- eda_plot_heatmap(dfClean, "GarageType", "NeighborhoodType", "SalePrice")
p3 <- eda_plot_heatmap(dfClean, "MSSubClass", "MSZoning", "SalePrice")
cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = list(p1, p2, p3), ncol = 1)

# number of combinations, and those with fewer than 10 properties
vCells <- map_int(list(p1, p2, p3), ~ nrow(.x$data))
vSparse <- map_int(list(p1, p2, p3), ~ sum(.x$data$n < 10))

Each tile shows the median SalePrice (by its color) and the number of properties. A tile is grey if it has fewer than 10 properties, because a median of so few properties is not reliable.

  • Some neighborhoods have more properties with a high OverallQual, so their prices are higher. But in Type4 neighborhoods, SalePrice clearly changes with the quality of the property.
  • It is less clear whether GarageType has a large effect by itself. Buyers seem to prefer built-in and attached garages, but NeighborhoodType explains most of the differences.
  • In both one-story and multi-story houses built after 1946, properties in low-density residential zones and floating village zones usually have higher prices.
  • Many combinations are rare: 11 of the 34 combinations of OverallQual and NeighborhoodType, and 20 of the 46 combinations of MSSubClass and MSZoning, have fewer than 10 properties. So we can compare only the common combinations reliably. Also, a model would find it hard to learn how these features work together.

Next Steps

This analysis gives us several results to use when we build models:

  • The total area, the overall quality, the neighborhood and the number of bathrooms have the strongest relationships with SalePrice.
  • Very skewed features, such as LotArea, should be transformed with a log before we fit linear models.
  • A few very large properties that sold at low prices, such as 524 and 1299, pull a straight-line fit strongly.
  • Many combinations of categories are rare, so a model cannot learn them reliably.

In Part 3, we use these results to build linear and non-linear models that predict the sale price, and we compare how well they work.

item.title: Diamonds - Part 1 - In the rough - An Exploratory Data Analysis
item.description:
Other posts in this series:

  • Diamonds - Part 2 - A cut above - Building Linear Models
  • Diamonds - Part 3 - A polished gem - Building Non-linear Models

In this case study, we explore the diamonds dataset. Then, in the next posts, we build models that predict the price of a diamond. A model is a formula that a computer learns from examples. Some models are linear (they use straight-line relationships) and some are non-linear (they can also learn curves).

Data Description

The diamonds dataset has almost 54,000 diamonds. For each diamond, it gives the price (in US dollars of 2008) and other attributes, such as the weight and the quality grades. We call each attribute a feature.

dfDescription <- tribble(~ Attribute, ~ Description,
                         "price", "price in 2008 USD",
                         "carat", "weight of a diamond (1 carat = 0.2 gms)",
                         "cut", "quality of the cut (Fair, Good, Very Good, Premium, Ideal)",
                         "color", "diamond color from D (best) to J (worst)",
                         "clarity", "a measurement of how clear the diamond is (I1 (worst), SI2, SI1, VS2, VS1, VVS2, VVS1, IF (best))",
                         "x", "length in mm",
                         "y", "width in mm",
                         "z", "depth in mm",
                         "depth", "total depth percentage = z/mean(x, y)",
                         "table", "width of the top of diamond relative to widest point")

knitr::kable(dfDescription)
Attribute Description
price price in 2008 USD
carat weight of a diamond (1 carat = 0.2 gms)
cut quality of the cut (Fair, Good, Very Good, Premium, Ideal)
color diamond color from D (best) to J (worst)
clarity a measurement of how clear the diamond is (I1 (worst), SI2, SI1, VS2, VS1, VVS2, VVS1, IF (best))
x length in mm
y width in mm
z depth in mm
depth total depth percentage = z/mean(x, y)
table width of the top of diamond relative to widest point

Data Summaries

vFeaturesCat <- dfInput %>% select_if(is.factor) %>% colnames() 
vFeaturesNum <- dfInput %>% select_if(is.numeric) %>% colnames()
visdat::vis_dat(dfInput) + theme_quant()

This chart shows all the features and their types. No values are missing in this dataset.

Next, we look at the numbers for each feature:

  • price: The average price of a diamond is about USD 4000. Many diamonds are much more expensive than most others. We call such unusual values outliers.
  • carat: The average weight is about 0.8 carat. About 75% of the diamonds weigh less than 1 carat. The 5 largest values show that there are many outliers at the high end.
  • cut: About 40% of the diamonds have an Ideal cut. Only 3% have a Fair cut. So the categories are not balanced: some categories have many more diamonds than others.
  • color: Most diamonds have a color grade from E to H. Fewer diamonds have the color grade J.
  • clarity: Most diamonds have a clarity grade from SI2 to VS1. About 1% have the worst grade, I1. Only about 3% have the best grade, IF.
  • depth: Most depth values are between 60 and 64. There are outliers at both the low end and the high end.
  • table: Most table values are between 54 and 65. There are outliers at both ends.
  • x: The length of the diamond in mm. Most values are between 4 and 8. Some values are 0, which means that nobody recorded them.
  • y: The width of the diamond in mm. Most values are between 3.5 and 8. 7 values are 0.
  • z: The depth of the diamond in mm. Most values are between 2.5 and 8.5. 20 values are 0.

Univariate Analysis: One Feature at a Time

In this section, we look at each feature by itself.

Numerical Features

eda_plot_histograms(dfInput, vFeaturesNum)

The plots show outliers in each feature. Let’s remove the outliers and plot the features again. We use a common rule: a value is an outlier if it is more than 2.5 interquartile ranges from the median. The median is the middle value: half the values are below it and half are above it. The interquartile range is the width of the middle half of the values. The outliers themselves have almost no effect on these two numbers, so the rule is reliable. A rule that uses the average would be less reliable, because the outliers pull the average towards them.

makeOutliersNA <- function(Z) {
  # values more than 2.5 interquartile ranges from the median become NA
  ifelse(flag_outliers(Z, nIQR = 2.5), NA, Z)
}

# convert outliers to NA values
dfInput <- dfInput %>% mutate_at(vFeaturesNum, makeOutliersNA)

eda_plot_histograms(dfInput, vFeaturesNum) + labs(title = "Histograms of numerical features excluding outliers")

Without the outliers, the ranges of the values are more reasonable. carat and price are right skewed: most values are small, and a few values are much larger.

Let’s plot price on a log scale. On a log scale, each step on the axis multiplies the value by the same amount (for example, from $100 to $1,000 to $10,000). This makes it easier to see the spread of skewed values:

eda_plot_histograms(dfInput, "price", nBins = 100, xLog = T, xLabelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1))

The plot has two peaks. This means that two price ranges are the most common: one just below USD 1000 and one near USD 5000. Interestingly, almost no diamonds cost about USD 1500. So the plot shows a big gap at that price.

Categorical Features

cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = map(vFeaturesCat, ~ eda_plot_column(dfInput, .x)), ncol = 2)

The plots clearly show that the categories of cut and clarity are not balanced.

Bivariate Analysis: Two Features at a Time

In this section, we look at how price changes with each of the other features.

Numerical-numerical

First, we measure the correlation of price with each numerical feature. A correlation is a number from -1 to 1. It tells how closely two features move together in a straight line. A value near 1 means that when one feature goes up, the other also goes up. A value near -1 means that the other goes down. A value near 0 means that there is no straight-line relationship.

eda_plot_correlation_matrix(dfInput[vFeaturesNum] %>% drop_na(), outlineVar = "price", plotTitle = "Clustered correlations of numerical features")

price has a very strong correlation with carat and with the dimensions x, y and z. These four features are also strongly correlated with each other, because they all measure the size of a diamond. So a linear model cannot easily separate their effects. table and depth have almost no correlation with price. So they are not useful to predict the price.

Now let’s look at the scatter plots. A scatter plot shows one dot for each diamond:

eda_plot_scatter(dfInput, vFeaturesNum, "price", yLimits = c(200, 15000), yLabelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1))

Without the outliers, price grows faster and faster as carat, x, y and z increase. So let’s plot price on a log scale:

eda_plot_scatter(dfInput, vFeaturesNum, "price", yLog = T, yLimits = c(200, 15000), yLabelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1))

On a log scale, log(price) has an approximately straight-line (linear) relationship with x, y and z. But its relationship with carat is still curved. Also, the spread (variance) of price increases as the diamonds get larger.

Can we change carat with a simple formula so that its relationship with log(price) becomes a straight line? We call such a change a transform. Let’s compare some common transforms. Each panel shows the R-squared of a straight line through the points. R-squared is a number from 0 to 1. It tells how much of the variation in log(price) the straight line explains. A higher value means that the line fits the points better:

p_transforms <- eda_plot_transforms(dfInput, "carat", "price")
p_transforms

# R-squared of each transform, in the order of the panels
vR2_carat <- p_transforms$data %>%
  distinct(transform, r_squared) %>%
  pull(r_squared) %>%
  set_names(c("identity", "log", "sqrt", "cuberoot"))

log(carat) gives the best straight-line fit, with an R-squared of 0.926. The cube root is second (0.919) and the square root is third (0.91). carat without a transform has the lowest R-squared, 0.862. So log(price) has an almost straight-line relationship with log(carat). This means that when the weight increases by a given percentage, the price increases by an approximately constant percentage. We will use this result when we create features for the models (Feature Engineering).

Numerical-Categorical

Let’s look at price for each category of the categorical features. A box plot shows the middle half of the prices as a box, with a line at the median:

cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = map(vFeaturesCat, ~ eda_plot_box(dfInput, .x, "price", yLimits = c(300, 8000), 
                                                               yLabelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1))), ncol = 3)

To show the trends better, the price axis of these box plots does not show the most expensive diamonds. The box plots are surprising: for cut, color and clarity, the median price usually goes down as the grade gets better. This is very strange. We will find the reason in the multivariate analysis.

  • The median price goes down steadily from a Fair cut to an Ideal cut.
  • For color, the median price goes down from J (worst) to G (middle grade). Then it goes up, and it goes down again for D (best).
  • For clarity, the median price goes up from I1 to SI2. Then it goes down steadily to IF.

Multivariate Analysis: Three or More Features at a Time

So far, we know that carat, x, y and z have the strongest relationship with price. The grades of cut, color and clarity also seem to have some effect on the median price. Let’s use scatter plots to look at these relationships together:

Numerical-Numerical-Categorical

cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = map(vFeaturesCat, ~ eda_plot_scatter_cat(dfInput, "carat", "price", .x, yLabelsScale = scales::dollar)), ncol = 2)

The dots overlap a lot. But for diamonds of the same carat weight, price clearly goes up as clarity gets better. color shows the same pattern, but it is weaker. cut does not show any effect.

So, for diamonds of the same weight, both color and clarity explain some of the differences in price.

All Features

Why do the diamonds with better grades seem cheaper in the bivariate analysis? To find out, we measure the association between every pair of features. An association tells how strongly two features are related. Here, we rank the grades of cut, color and clarity from worst to best. Then we can compare them with the numerical features with Spearman’s rank correlation. This correlation uses the ranks of the values instead of the values themselves, so it also works for grades:

eda_plot_association_matrix(dfInput, method = "spearman", ordinalAsNumeric = T, outlineVar = "price",
                            plotTitle = "Spearman correlations, with grades ranked from worst to best")

mAssoc <- association_matrix(dfInput, method = "spearman", ordinalAsNumeric = T)
  • carat has a negative correlation with clarity (-0.37) and with color (-0.24). This means that diamonds with better grades are usually smaller.
  • price has a very strong correlation with carat (0.96). So price also has a negative correlation with clarity (-0.21) and with color (-0.13).
  • carat, x, y and z form a tight group, and they are almost perfectly correlated with each other. So, to predict the price, these features give almost the same information.

Categorical-Numerical-Numerical

In the scatter plots, the dots overlap too much to show how much each grade matters. So let’s compare grades among diamonds of similar weight. We split the diamonds into four groups (bins) of equal size by carat. Then we plot price for each grade in each group:

lBinPlots <- map(c("clarity", "color", "cut"), ~ eda_plot_box_by_bins(dfInput, .x, "price", "carat", yLog = T,
                                                                       yLabelsScale = scales::label_dollar(accuracy = 1)))
cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = lBinPlots, ncol = 1)

# median price by grade within each carat bin
get_bin_medians <- function(p) {
  p$data %>%
    group_by(bin = as.integer(bin), grade = as.character(x)) %>%
    summarise(median = median(y), .groups = "drop")
}
dfBinMedians_clarity <- get_bin_medians(lBinPlots[[1]])
bin_median <- function(dfMedians, binNum, gradeName) {
  scales::dollar(dfMedians$median[dfMedians$bin == binNum & dfMedians$grade == gradeName], accuracy = 1)
}

# median carat by clarity
dfCarat_clarity <- dfInput %>% group_by(clarity) %>% summarise(carat = median(carat, na.rm = T))

These plots explain the strange box plots of the bivariate analysis:

  • In each carat group, the median price usually goes up as clarity gets better. The effect is clearest for the heaviest diamonds: the median price goes from $3,985 for I1 to $10,332 for IF. The prices of the best grades (VVS2 to IF) are close to each other, and they are not always in order.
  • In each group, price also goes up as color gets better from J to G. But the best grades (G to D) have about the same price. For the heaviest diamonds, D and E are even a little cheaper than G.
  • cut does not show a clear trend, even for diamonds of similar weight.

Diamonds with better grades seem cheaper overall because they are usually smaller. The median weight of an I1 diamond is 1.07 carat. The median weight of an IF diamond is only 0.35 carat. So carat is a confounder: it is related to both price and the grades, and it hides the true effect of the grades. To measure the effect of clarity or color, we must compare diamonds of similar weight.

Next, let’s check whether table and depth affect price together with color and clarity:

dfFeatures <- expand_grid(feat1 = c("depth","table"), feat2 = c("color","clarity")) %>% arrange(desc(feat2))
cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = map2(dfFeatures$feat1, dfFeatures$feat2, 
                                   ~ eda_plot_scatter_cat(dfInput, .x, "price", .y, yLabelsScale = scales::dollar)), nrow = 2)

These plots do not show any pattern. So table and depth do not help to predict price.

Categorical-Categorical-Numerical

Does clarity together with cut or color tell us more about price? A heatmap answers this question. It shows a grid of tiles, one for each combination of two categories. The color of each tile shows the median price of the diamonds in that combination:

cowplot::plot_grid(plotlist = map(c("cut","color"), ~ eda_plot_heatmap(dfInput, .x, "clarity", "price")), nrow = 2)

The second heatmap is more interesting. From the bottom left to the top right, the grades of color and clarity get better, and the median price usually goes down. Again, this is the opposite of what we expect, because the diamonds with the best color and clarity should be the most expensive. As we saw above, the reason is that diamonds with better grades are usually smaller.

For cut and clarity, the median prices do not show a clear pattern. Each tile shows its number of diamonds. One combination (Fair cut and IF clarity) has fewer than 10 diamonds. Its tile is grey, because a median of so few diamonds is not reliable.

Summary

Here is what we found in this exploratory data analysis (EDA), which is the first study of a dataset before we build models:

  • price is right skewed. On a log scale, it has two peaks, so diamonds are popular in two different price ranges.
  • carat: about 75% of the diamonds weigh less than 1 carat. The spread of prices increases with weight. log(price) has an almost straight-line relationship with log(carat).
  • cut is not balanced: about 40% of the diamonds have an Ideal cut.
  • color is not balanced: only about 5% of the diamonds have the color grade J.
  • clarity is not balanced at the two ends: only 1.5% of the diamonds have the grade I1, and only 3.3% have the grade IF.
  • price has a strong correlation with carat and with the dimensions x, y and z. table and depth have almost no correlation with price.
  • For diamonds of the same weight, clarity and color explain some of the differences in price. Overall, better grades seem to lower the price only because diamonds with better grades are usually smaller. cut has little effect.
save(vFeaturesCat, vFeaturesNum, makeOutliersNA, file = "diamondClean.Rda")
